chapters.title: Start here: Test 3, and how this episode works
Case L: Jack's noise-induced hearing loss

show.ask: Jack works in a very noisy open-plan office and has listened to loud music for a long time to drown it out. He now has trouble hearing and understanding. Which parts of the ear are damaged, and where are they? How does loud noise over time damage them, and how does that lead to deafness? What kind of deafness is this, and how does it compare with the other kind?
show.hook: CORTI → SNAP → SILENT → SENSORINEURAL: where it breaks, how, what that does, what kind.

groups.h: Which parts are damaged, and where?
t: Hair cells are damaged
They sit in the organ of Corti
on the basilar membrane, in the cochlea of the inner ear

groups.h: How does loud noise damage them?
t: Loud sound = high-amplitude waves
The hairs bend against the tectorial membrane
Over time they break off
85 dB or more over time; 130 dB at once
No nerve impulses go down nerve VIII to the brain
Hair cells do not grow back, so it is permanent

groups.h: What kind of deafness, and the other kind?
t: Sensorineural deafness: damage from the cochlea to the brain
The other kind is conduction: sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear
e.g. earwax or glue ear; often reversible

chapters.title: Case L, question 5: otosclerosis

show.ask: A CT scan of Jack's ears shows no signs of otosclerosis. What kind of deafness would otosclerosis have caused, what specific structure of the ear is damaged by that condition, in what part of the ear is this structure(s) found and how does this damage impact hearing?
show.hook: OSSICLES STUCK → no VIBRATION → CONDUCTION deafness.

t: Conduction deafness: sound cannot reach the internal ear
The ossicles: malleus, incus, stapes
Patton: irregularities in the stapes
They sit in the middle ear
They pass the vibrations on to the oval window
The ossicles become attached to the walls of the middle ear
That interferes with the vibrations: they cannot amplify the sound
Inner ear and hair cells are fine: the skull bones still conduct

chapters.title: Case 11: Pania's milk coming in

show.ask: Pania is 2 days postpartum and her milk is just 'coming in'. Two hormones are involved in the production and release of breast milk: for each, say where it is made or secreted from, what stimulates it, and its function. Describe the structure of the mammary gland and the path milk takes out of the breast. What type of gland is it, and what happens to the breasts in pregnancy as progesterone rises?
show.hook: PROlactin PROduces, OXYtocin lets it OUT. Suckling fires both. Oestrogen = the pipes, progesterone = the factories.

t: Prolactin: from the anterior pituitary
It stimulates milk production by the alveolar cells
Oxytocin: made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary
It stimulates milk release (let-down): myoepithelial cells contract
A neural stimulus: the baby suckling (or its cry)
Mammary glands are modified sweat glands
15-25 lobes around the nipple, each with lobules of alveoli
Areola around the nipple; suspensory ligaments hold the breast
Alveoli → alveolar ducts → lactiferous ducts → nipple
Progesterone develops the lobules and alveoli (the milk factories)
Oestrogen grows the ducts
Before pregnancy there are ducts but no glandular tissue

chapters.title: Case 11, question 5: the hormone tick table

show.ask: Complete the following table about the roles of hormones in breast development, milk production and release by ticking the appropriate boxes (progesterone, oestrogen, prolactin, oxytocin): stimulates growth of milk ducts and glands · increases blood flow to the breasts · stimulate development of the lobules and alveoli · stimulates milk production and the development of mammary glands · stimulates milk ejection by making the myoepithelial cells around the milk ducts contract, squeezing the milk towards the nipple.
show.hook: PIPES (oestrogen), FACTORIES (progesterone), FILL (prolactin), TAPS (oxytocin).

t: Ducts and glands grow: oestrogen + progesterone
Blood flow to the breasts: oestrogen (the tool's tick)
Lobules and alveoli: progesterone
Milk production: prolactin
Ejection, the myoepithelial cells squeeze: oxytocin

chapters.title: Pedigree charts: she says they will be tested

show.ask: Explain how you work out the mode of inheritance from a pedigree chart, how you assign genotypes, and how you find the chance of another affected child. Use an autosomal dominant family as your example: an affected father and an unaffected mother who have both affected and unaffected children.
show.hook: SKIP? (skips = recessive) · BOYS vs GIRLS? (even = autosomal) · RECESSIVES first · PUNNETT the parents: Bb × bb = 50%.

t: Squares = males, circles = females, shaded = affected
In every generation, never skips = dominant
Skips a generation = recessive
Count males vs females: equal = autosomal
A father passing it to his son rules out X-linked
X-linked dominant: affected fathers pass it to all their daughters
Label the homozygous recessives first (bb)
Father Bb (he has unaffected children); mother bb
Punnett square of the parents: Bb × bb
2 Bb : 2 bb = a 50% chance for each child

chapters.title: Huntington's disease

show.ask: Explain Huntington's disease as a genetic disease: its cause, how it damages the body, how it is inherited, and the chance of an affected child when one parent is Hh and the other is hh.
show.hook: Chromosome 4 → CAG STUTTER → TOXIC protein in the brain → ONE H is enough: Hh × hh = 50%.

t: A mutated gene on chromosome 4
Chromosome 4 is an autosome
CAG repeated 36-120 times (normal: 10-35)
It makes an abnormal huntingtin protein, which is toxic
It builds up in the brain: movement, thinking and memory suffer
Autosomal dominant: one copy (Hh) is enough
No healthy carriers: Hh is affected, only hh is not
It shows in every generation
Hh × hh → 2 Hh : 2 hh
Each child has a 50% chance

chapters.title: Glaucoma and cataracts

show.ask: Explain glaucoma and cataracts: which part of the eye each one affects, what goes wrong, and how it affects vision.
show.hook: GLAUCOMA = PRESSURE: the drain blocks and the nerve is crushed. CATARACT = a CLOUDY LENS.

groups.h: Glaucoma: where, what goes wrong, what it does
t: Glaucoma is a problem with the aqueous humor
The ciliary body makes it; the canal of Schlemm drains it
Drain blocked → fluid builds up → intraocular pressure rises
Pressure damages the retina and optic nerve → blindness

groups.h: Cataract: where, what goes wrong, what it does
t: A cataract affects the lens
Its proteins denature, so it goes cloudy (opaque)
Vision goes blurred and yellowed, with glare
Treated by surgery that replaces the lens

chapters.title: The words of genetics

show.ask: Find the terms by matching them to the correct definition: homozygous, heterozygous, allele, dominant, recessive, genotype, phenotype, autosomal, X-linked, locus, chromosomes, genome, autosome, sex chromosome, variation, inheritance.

t: Homozygous: the alleles of the genotype are the same
Heterozygous: the alleles of the genotype are different
Allele: a different version of a gene
Dominant: will always appear in the phenotype
Recessive: appears only if no other alleles are present
Genotype: the alleles an individual has inherited
Phenotype: how the traits are expressed and seen
Autosomal: a disease gene on chromosomes 1–22
X-linked: a disease gene on the X; more males affected
Locus: where a gene sits on a chromosome
Chromosomes: lengths of DNA carrying many genes, in pairs
Genome: all the DNA in the nucleus
Autosome: a chromosome numbered 1–22
Sex chromosome: the X or the Y
Variation: differences in genes across a population
Inheritance: how genes pass from parents to children

chapters.title: Using a Punnett square

show.ask: Explain how a Punnett square is used to predict offspring. Work a Bb × Bb cross (brown eyes B dominant over blue b) and a codominant blood group cross (Iᴬi × Iᴮi).
show.hook: One parent ACROSS THE TOP, one DOWN THE SIDE, one letter from each into every box.

t: Alleles come in pairs, one from each parent
It shows all the possible combinations: the probability of each
One parent across the top, the other down the side
Bb × Bb → 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb
25% homozygous dominant, 50% heterozygous, 25% homozygous recessive
Phenotypes: 75% brown : 25% blue
Codominance: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both expressed; i (O) is recessive
Iᴬi × Iᴮi → AB, A, B and O, 25% each

chapters.title: Patterns of inheritance

show.ask: Briefly explain these patterns of inheritance, with an example of each: codominance, incomplete dominance, polygenic inheritance and mitochondrial inheritance.
show.hook: CO = BOTH show (AB). INCOMPLETE = a BLEND (sickle cell). POLY = MANY genes (height). MITO = MUM only.

t: Both alleles are fully expressed
e.g. ABO blood groups: A and B together give AB
One allele does not completely mask the other: intermediate
e.g. sickle cell: carriers have normal and sickle cells
Many genes control one trait: a continuous range (bell curve)
e.g. height, skin colour
Mitochondrial DNA passes only by the mother, to all her children
Severity varies: the bottleneck effect (a threshold)

chapters.title: Multiple alleles, blood groups and X-linked genes

show.ask: Briefly explain multiple allele inheritance and sex-linked (X-linked) inheritance, using the right genetics terms.

t: Multiple alleles: a trait controlled by more than two alleles, like the ABO blood groups
Three alleles, A, B and O: six genotypes, four blood groups
A and B are codominant; both are dominant over O
AO × BO gives A, B, AB and O, 25% each
X-linked: the gene is on the X, and the Y has no matching allele
So one copy shows in a male; a female needs two
Only females can be carriers
Carrier mum × normal dad: 50% of sons affected, no daughters
Affected dad × normal mum: no affected sons; every daughter a carrier

chapters.title: DNA, chromosomes and mutations

show.ask: Understand the structure and function of DNA and RNA (review from BN1), and define some ways genetic abnormalities occur, including mutation, genetic disease and aneuploidy.

t: DNA: deoxyribonucleic acid, a double helix; A pairs with T, G with C
DNA stores the genetic code and passes traits on: the molecule of heredity
RNA: one strand, ribose, uracil for thymine; carries the code out to make proteins
Chromosome: coiled DNA with many genes; gene: a segment coding for a trait or protein
Gamete 23 chromosomes; zygote 46, half from each parent
Crossing over (a chiasma) can separate linked genes in meiosis
Mutation: a permanent change in a gene's DNA code
Genetic disease: from a faulty gene, e.g. Huntington's (dominant), cystic fibrosis, Tay-Sachs (recessive)
Aneuploidy: an abnormal number of chromosomes (Down, Turner)

chapters.title: Karyotypes and aneuploidy

show.ask: What is a human karyotype and how many chromosomes does it show? What is aneuploidy? Give two examples and explain how aneuploidy arises.
show.hook: 46 = 23 PAIRS. ONE TOO MANY (Down, 47) or ONE TOO FEW (Turner, 45) = pairs failing to split in meiosis.

t: A picture of the chromosomes in numbered homologous pairs
46 chromosomes = 23 pairs
22 pairs of autosomes + XX or XY
Aneuploidy = an abnormal number of chromosomes
Down syndrome = trisomy 21: 47 chromosomes
Turner syndrome: 45, only one X
Non-disjunction in meiosis
Pairs fail to separate, so a gamete gets one too many or few

chapters.title: Detecting and treating genetic disease

show.ask: Explain some ways genetic abnormalities are detected, including genetic testing and fetal testing, and what genetic engineering and gene therapy are.
show.hook: LOOK (blood test, karyotype) → SAMPLE the baby (CVS early, amnio later) → CHANGE DNA (engineering) → TREAT (gene therapy).

t: Genetic testing reads a person's DNA (a blood sample)
e.g. a karyotype or a CGH-array
Chorionic villus sampling (CVS): the placenta, 8-12 weeks
Amniocentesis: amniotic fluid, 14-20 weeks
Both check the fetal cells for disorders
Genetic engineering: deliberate alteration of DNA
e.g. bacteria altered to make insulin
Gene therapy: treatment of a genetic disease by inserting genetic material

chapters.title: The three regions of the ear

show.ask: What are the three regions of the ear? Describe their structures and functions.
show.hook: OUTER collects, MIDDLE amplifies, INNER senses: the cochlea hears, the vestibular apparatus balances.

t: Pinna, external auditory canal (cerumen), tympanic membrane
It collects sound onto the eardrum and helps locate it
Air-filled, in the temporal bone; holds the ossicles
It amplifies sound onto the oval window
The Eustachian tube equalises pressure
Two small muscles dampen loud sounds
Bony labyrinth (perilymph) around a membranous labyrinth (endolymph)
The cochlea: hearing (organ of Corti)
The vestibular apparatus: equilibrium (balance)

chapters.title: How hearing happens

show.ask: Discuss how hearing occurs in humans, from the sound wave arriving at the ear to the sound being perceived.
show.hook: COLLECT → AMPLIFY → RIPPLE → BEND → FIRE → HEAR: outer ear, middle ear, inner ear, nerve, brain.

t: The pinna collects sound; the tympanic membrane vibrates
The ossicles (malleus → incus → stapes) pass it on
and amplify it onto the oval window
The vibration moves the perilymph, then the endolymph
The basilar membrane moves
Hair cells of the organ of Corti bend against the tectorial membrane

groups.h: To the brain: fire and hear
t: Bending = transduction into nerve impulses
along nerve VIII to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe

chapters.title: Static and dynamic equilibrium

show.ask: What is the difference between static and dynamic equilibrium? How and where is each detected?
show.hook: STATIC = GRAVITY and straight lines: the VESTIBULE, stones slide. DYNAMIC = SPINNING: the CANALS, a gel cap swings.

t: Hair cells in the vestibular apparatus fire when their hairs bend
Signals go along nerve VIII to the cerebellum
Static: head position in response to gravity and straight-line movement
Detected by the maculae in the utricle and saccule
Otoliths (ear stones) slide when the head tilts
Dynamic: balance while the head is rotating
Detected by the crista ampullaris in each semicircular canal
Rotation swings the gel cupula, bending the hairs

chapters.title: The three layers of the eye

show.ask: What are the three layers (tunics) of the eye? Give their structures and functions.
show.hook: Outside in: TOUGH COAT (sclera, cornea) → BLOOD COAT (choroid, ciliary body, iris) → SEEING COAT (retina).

t: Sclera: white, protects the eye, anchors the muscles
Cornea: clear, does about 80% of the refraction
Choroid: rich in blood vessels, nourishes the eye
Ciliary body: holds the lens and changes its shape
Iris: its muscles control pupil size
The retina's outer pigmented layer absorbs light
Photoreceptors (rods and cones) → bipolar cells → ganglion cells
Their axons leave as the optic nerve (II)
Photoreceptors turn light into nerve impulses

chapters.title: The retina: rods, cones and colour blindness

show.ask: What receptors are impacted by colour blindness?

t: Photoreceptors, specifically the CONES of the eye
The cones are found mostly in the macula lutea and the fovea centralis

show.ask: What are the receptors for light, where exactly are they found, and how do rods and cones differ?

t: Photoreceptors: rods and cones, in the retina
Cones: macula lutea, packed in the fovea centralis; bright light, colour, sharp images (photopic)
Rods: none in the fovea, more towards the edges; dim light, black and white (scotopic)
Up to 100 rods share one ganglion cell: sensitive, but less sharp
Pigments differ by their opsin protein; light hyperpolarises the photoreceptor
The optic disc has no photoreceptors: the blind spot
Afterimage: the retina's signal persists after the light has gone

chapters.title: Near vision: the three changes

show.ask: What changes occur in the eye to allow near vision? How is this undone for distant vision?
show.hook: Near = BULGE, SHRINK, CROSS. Far = all three undo.

t: The ciliary muscle contracts
so the lens bulges (gets rounder)
The pupils constrict
The eyes converge (turn inwards)
Ciliary muscle relaxes, lens flattens, pupils dilate
Near light arrives diverging; from over 6 m it is parallel

chapters.title: Myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism

show.ask: Explain how myopia, emmetropia and hyperopia differ and how each error is corrected. What is astigmatism?
show.hook: MY-opia: MY world is close, focus falls SHORT → conCAVE. HYPER-opia: focus overshoots → conVEX.

t: Emmetropia: light focused on the retina
Myopia: distant light focuses in front of the retina
The eyeball is too long; far things blur
Fixed with a concave lens, which diverges the light
Hyperopia: near light focuses behind the retina
The eyeball is too short; near things blur
Fixed with a convex lens, which converges the light
The cornea or lens is curved unevenly
Light focuses at several points: blurred at all distances
Fixed with glasses, contacts or laser surgery

chapters.title: Waves: light and sound

show.ask: Explain amplitude, wavelength and frequency and how we experience each. Compare light and sound waves, and explain the difference between reflection and refraction of light.
show.hook: TALL = loud or bright. PEAK TO PEAK = colour. HOW MANY = pitch. Reflection BOUNCES, refraction BENDS.

t: Amplitude = the wave's height: loudness (dB), brightness
Wavelength = one peak to the next: light's colour
Frequency = waves per second (Hz): sound's pitch
Higher frequency = shorter wavelength
Light: electromagnetic, needs no medium
Sound: a mechanical pressure wave, needs a medium
Reflection: light bounces back, e.g. a mirror
Refraction: light bends as it slows down in a different density
e.g. a rainbow, or the cornea and lens focusing light

chapters.title: Taste: the taste buds

show.ask: Briefly describe the structure of the taste buds and discuss the physiology of taste sensation.
show.hook: BUDS on PAPILLAE → CHEMICALS in saliva → VII / IX / X → INSULA.

t: Taste buds sit on the papillae of the tongue
Papillae: fungiform, vallate, filiform, foliate
Each bud: gustatory cells in a supporting capsule
Gustatory hairs poke into the taste pore
A chemical sense: chemoreceptors, chemicals dissolved in saliva
Five tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami
Facial (VII) front 2/3; glossopharyngeal (IX) back 1/3; vagus (X)
→ brainstem → thalamus → insula and frontal lobe
Flavour = taste + smell: aroma rises into the nasal cavity

chapters.title: Smell: the olfactory epithelium

show.ask: Briefly describe the structure of the olfactory epithelium and discuss the physiology of olfaction.
show.hook: ROOF → MUCUS → RECEPTOR → CRIBRIFORM (I) → BULB → TEMPORAL.

t: In the roof of the nasal cavity: you sniff to reach it
Olfactory receptor neurons with olfactory cilia
plus supporting cells and basal cells, which replace the neurons
Odourants dissolve in the mucus, then bind the receptors
Axons through the cribriform plate: cranial nerve I
They synapse in the olfactory bulb
Bulbs under the frontal lobe; the olfactory tract carries on
Primary olfactory cortex, in the temporal lobe, names the smell
Amygdala (emotion), hippocampus (memory)
Total loss: anosmia; partial: hyposmia

chapters.title: The male reproductive system: every structure and its job

show.ask: Make sure you can label all the structures of the male reproductive system and state their functions.

t: Function: produce sperm and testosterone; deliver sperm into the female tract
Scrotum: keeps the testes 3 °C cooler; dartos (smooth) wrinkles it, cremaster (skeletal) lifts the testes
Testes: seminiferous tubules make sperm; Leydig cells make testosterone; Sertoli cells nourish sperm
Epididymis: stores the sperm, where they mature and become motile
Vas deferens: carries sperm to the ampulla; cut in a vasectomy
Seminal vesicles: 60% of semen, alkaline, fructose and prostaglandins; form the ejaculatory duct with the vas
Prostate: under the bladder, round the urethra; about a third of semen, citric acid, PSA
Bulbourethral glands: clear mucus that neutralises acidic urine before ejaculation
Urethra: prostatic, membranous, spongy; carries urine and semen
Penis: delivers sperm; corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum (erectile), glans, prepuce

chapters.title: Semen, sperm count, erection and ejaculation

show.ask: Describe the composition of semen and normal sperm count in relation to sterility. (Reproductive 6)

t: Semen: 60% seminal vesicles, 30% prostate, 10% sperm and the rest
2 to 5 mL per ejaculation, 50 to 130 million sperm per mL
Her key: as many as 750 million sperm in one ejaculation
Sterility: a count below about 20 to 25 million per mL
Carries, feeds (fructose, citrate), protects and activates the sperm; alkaline
Prostaglandins thin cervical mucus and set off reverse peristalsis in the uterus

show.ask: Describe the physiology of the male sexual response and relate it to erectile dysfunction. (Reproductive 5)

t: Erection, parasympathetic: nitric oxide → arterioles dilate → corpora cavernosa fill → veins squashed
Corpus spongiosum keeps the urethra open
Ejaculation, sympathetic: ducts and glands contract, bladder sphincter closes, bulbospongiosus pumps semen out
Erectile dysfunction: unable to attain an erection
Viagra blocks PDE5, which breaks down cGMP

chapters.title: Making sperm and eggs

show.ask: Describe the gamete production process in males and females. What hormone from the brain drives this?
show.hook: SPERM: puberty, non-stop, 1 → 4. EGG: before birth, pauses, one a month, finishes only if a sperm gets in, 1 → 1. Both: FSH.

t: Spermatogenesis: seminiferous tubules, continuously from puberty
Spermatogonia divide by mitosis → primary spermatocytes
meiosis I, then meiosis II → 4 sperm
Oogenesis starts in fetal life
Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I until puberty
From puberty, one a month completes meiosis I and is ovulated
Meiosis II finishes only if a sperm enters: 1 ovum
FSH from the anterior pituitary (with LH)

chapters.title: The female reproductive system: every structure and its job

show.ask: Make sure you can label all the structures of the female reproductive system and state their functions.

t: Function: produce ova and the sex hormones; support fertilisation, pregnancy and birth
Ovaries: follicles hold the oocytes, in the cortex; secrete oestrogen and progesterone
Fallopian tubes: fimbriae draw the oocyte in; site of fertilisation; cilia and peristalsis carry it to the uterus
Uterus: fundus, body, isthmus, cervix; receives the embryo and nourishes it until the placenta forms
Wall: perimetrium, myometrium (smooth muscle), endometrium (functionalis shed, basalis regrows)
Cervix: the neck; its mucus blocks bacteria
Vagina: cervix to outside; birth canal, menstrual flow, copulation; acidic
Vulva: mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoris (erectile; matches the glans penis)

chapters.title: The ovarian and uterine cycles

show.ask: Describe the phases of the ovarian and uterine cycles in the female and how the hormones link them.
show.hook: OVARY: GROW (FSH) → POP (LH) → YELLOW BODY (progesterone) → WHITE SCAR. UTERUS: SHED → REBUILD (oestrogen) → GET READY (progesterone).

t: Follicular phase (days 1-14): FSH makes a follicle grow
primordial → primary → secondary → Graafian
The follicle secretes oestrogen
Ovulation (about day 14): an LH surge releases the secondary oocyte
Luteal phase: the corpus luteum secretes progesterone
No pregnancy: it becomes the corpus albicans
Menstrual phase (days 1-5): progesterone falls
Spiral arteries spasm; the stratum functionalis is shed
Proliferative phase (6-14): oestrogen rebuilds the lining
Secretory phase (15-28): progesterone readies it for implantation
No implantation: progesterone falls, menstruation starts again

chapters.title: Male versus female: the comparison table

show.ask: Tabulate the differences between the male and female reproductive systems, looking at: the function of LH, the function of FSH, the timing of gamete production, the size of the gametes, the timing of meiosis and the mobility of the gametes.
show.hook: Six rows, female vs male, one line each: LH, FSH, timing, size, meiosis, moving.

t: Female: triggers ovulation
Male: Leydig cells make testosterone
Female: follicle development
Male: spermatogenesis (via the Sertoli cells)
Female: starts in fetal life; eggs from puberty to menopause
Male: from puberty, for life
Egg: the largest body cell
Sperm: the smallest
Female: stops and starts; 1 egg
Male: continuous; 4 sperm
Egg: cannot move, carried by cilia
Sperm: motile, swims with a tail

chapters.title: Hormonal control of sperm, and testosterone

show.ask: Describe the hormonal control of spermatogenesis, and the physiological effects of testosterone during puberty.
show.hook: GnRH → FSH + LH. L-T: LH → Leydig → Testosterone. S-I: FSH → Sertoli → sperm care + Inhibin.

t: Hypothalamus → GnRH → anterior pituitary
which releases FSH and LH
LH → Leydig (interstitial) cells → testosterone
Testosterone enhances spermatogenesis
FSH → Sertoli (sustentacular) cells, which nourish the sperm
Testosterone switches off GnRH and LH
Inhibin (from Sertoli cells) switches off FSH
Grows the reproductive organs to adult size
Pubic, axillary and facial hair; a deeper voice
More bone density and skeletal muscle mass; libido

show.ask: What are the functions of the sex hormone testosterone in males and females respectively? (her student-marked quiz, Q21)

t: Females too: the adrenal glands make testosterone
Males: libido, bone mass, fat distribution, muscle mass and strength, red blood cells and sperm
It is the basis of libido in both males and females

chapters.title: Oestrogen, progesterone and the pill

show.ask: Describe the physiological effects of oestrogen and progesterone, including the female secondary sex characteristics, and explain how the contraceptive pill prevents pregnancy.
show.hook: OESTROGEN BUILDS (organs, breasts, hips, lining). PROGESTERONE PREPARES (lining, milk glands). THE PILL: no egg, a mucus plug, a thin lining.

t: Oestrogen rises at puberty and drives follicle growth
It grows the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina
Breast growth; fat on the hips and breasts
A wider, lighter pelvis; axillary and pubic hair
It rebuilds the endometrium (proliferative phase)
Progesterone (corpus luteum) readies the lining for implantation
In pregnancy it develops the breast lobules and alveoli
The contraceptive pill: synthetic oestrogen and progestin
It stops ovulation and thickens the cervical mucus
and thins the endometrium, so an egg cannot implant

chapters.title: The female sexual response, and four words

show.ask: Describe the female sexual response: erection and orgasm, according to the effects of parasympathetic and sympathetic nerve impulses. (Reproductive 13, self-directed)

t: Similar to the male's
The clitoris and vaginal mucosa engorge with blood
The vestibular glands lubricate the vestibule
The nipples harden (sympathetic, her slide)
Orgasm: muscle tension, faster pulse, higher blood pressure, rhythmic uterine contractions

show.ask: Explain the terms menarche, menopause, amenorrhoea and dysmenorrhoea. (Reproductive 14)

t: Menarche: the first menstrual period, as the reproductive hormones start surging
Menopause: the reproductive hormones decline, and the cycles become erratic, then stop
Amenorrhoea: no menstrual periods
Dysmenorrhoea: painful periods

chapters.title: Start here: the final, and how this episode works
Case 2: the aftereffects of lymph node removal
chapters.scen: Exam case 2 · The aftereffects of lymph node removal — Aleki and Vicky visit their friend, Mary who had undergone a right mastectomy for cancer a fortnight ago. Mary mentioned the cancer had spread to the lymph nodes and that some axillary lymph nodes were also removed. She complained of swelling in the right arm after the surgery. Her friend, who is good with mirimiri and massage offers to help massage her arm, which helps to bring down the swelling.

show.ask: What are the major functions of the lymphatic system, which the lymph is a part of?
show.hook: DIGEST fat, DEFEND the body, DRAIN the tissues.

t: Digestive: lacteals in the gut absorb dietary fat
Immunological: the immune response
thymus (T cells mature), bone marrow (B cells mature)
lymph nodes: where immune cells meet and coordinate
Fluid balance: drains excess tissue fluid
and returns it to the venous system

show.ask: What is the role of the axillary lymph nodes in the spread of cancer? Explain.
show.hook: Cancer escapes into the lymph; the SENTINEL node is checked first.

t: Spread of cancer = metastasis
Cancer cells in the lymphatic system can reach any part of the body
The axillary (armpit) nodes are checked for cancer cells
The first, closest to the breast, is the sentinel node
Cancer there = it has spread; none = likely still in the breast

show.ask: Why did Mary develop swelling in the right arm after mastectomy? You will need to think about fluid dynamics, and what causes fluid to move into or still in the interstitial spaces (tissue space).
show.hook: Nodes out → drain BLOCKED → fluid stays → LYMPHOEDEMA.

t: Removing the lymph nodes: the arm's drainage is blocked
Normally tissue fluid drains back at the subclavian vein
Now the lymphatic vessels fill and cannot drain the tissue
The swelling is lymphoedema

show.ask: The role of the axillary lymph nodes in the spread of cancer is ____. The Spread of cancer is known as [a], so if cancerous cells detach themselves from their origin (for tumor for example), and get into the lymphatic system they could potentially get to any part of the body. Checking the armpit lymph nodes, since the breast drains to them, can give an indication of whether cancer has spread. If they have no cancer cells, it shows that the cancer is ____. The swelling in Mary's right arm after mastectomy is a sign that ____.

t: 1. metastasis
2. limited to the breast
3. the lymph drainage is hampered by the surgery

chapters.title: Case 3, part 1: Ane's asthma attack
chapters.scen: Exam case 3 · Asthma — Ane has had severe asthma since they were young. During a particularly bad asthma attack, Ane is experiencing difficulty breathing, particularly on the out-breath. Ane’s asthma is often triggered by small particles of pollen that manage to make their way into their lungs despite the protective features designed to keep them out. Ane makes sure to have their Salbutamol inhaler, which helps to relieve the symptoms of their asthma attack.

show.ask: What term is used to describe difficulty breathing?
show.hook: DYS = bad, PNOEA = breathing.

t: Dyspnoea: dys (bad) + pnoea (breathing)

show.ask: What is happening in Ane’s lungs to make breathing difficult?
show.hook: SQUEEZE, SWELL, SLIME.

t: Bronchoconstriction: the airway smooth muscle has contracted
Inflammation: the airway wall is thick with swelling
More mucus secretion: less room for air

show.ask: How is Ane’s ventilation and airway resistance impacted?
show.hook: Narrow pipes: HIGH resistance, HARDER work, EXTRA muscles.

t: Airway resistance is high → harder to breathe
It needs a greater pressure difference → dyspnoea
Accessory respiratory muscles are recruited
An increase in the work of breathing

show.ask: How does an inhaler help when Ane is having an asthma attack?
show.hook: The reliever RELAXES the airway; the preventer calms inflammation.

t: A reliever is a bronchodilator
The airway smooth muscle is forced to relax, so the airway widens
(A preventer is a corticosteroid: anti-inflammatory)

show.ask: The term used to describe difficulty breathing is ____. The best answer would be: Ane’s breathing is made difficult because asthma makes the bronchi and bronchiole become obstructed by ____. An inhaler helps during an asthma attack because it makes the airways ____. One mechanism that the body uses to keep dust and small particles out of the lungs and formed by the pseudostratified columnar epithelium lining of the airways is the ____.

t: 1. dyspnea
2. swelling and mucus accumulation
3. dilate
4. muco-ciliary escalator

chapters.title: Case 3, part 2: keeping dust out, and bringing the pressure down
chapters.scen: Exam case 3 · Asthma — Ane has had severe asthma since they were young. During a particularly bad asthma attack, Ane is experiencing difficulty breathing, particularly on the out-breath. Ane’s asthma is often triggered by small particles of pollen that manage to make their way into their lungs despite the protective features designed to keep them out. Ane makes sure to have their Salbutamol inhaler, which helps to relieve the symptoms of their asthma attack.

show.ask: How does the body usually keep dust and small particles out of the lungs? There are several mechanisms for this!
show.hook: STICK and SWEEP, FILTER, COUGH.

t: Mucus and cilia: the muco-ciliary escalator
Nasal hairs filter; particles stick in mucus
The carina triggers the cough reflex
The epiglottis keeps large objects out of the trachea

show.ask: The muco-cillary escalator is one of the mechanism. How does the muco-cillary escalator work?
show.hook: Mucus STICKS it, cilia SWEEP it up and out.

t: Cilia line the respiratory epithelium
They beat to sweep mucus up and out of the airways
Mucus is sticky: dust is trapped in it

show.ask: Smoking damages this escalator – how would this impact a smoker?
show.hook: Cilia DAMAGED → mucus STUCK → smoker's COUGH.

t: The cilia are damaged
so mucus cannot be moved up and out
A smoker’s cough develops to replace them

show.ask: Ane’s blood pressure was high due to their fight or flight response. What process helps to return their blood pressure back to normal after their asthma attack? (Think the full process!)
show.hook: STRETCH → MEDULLA: brake ON, accelerator OFF → vagus slows → vessels WIDEN.

t: Carotid and aortic baroreceptors (stretch receptors) pick up high pressure
To the medulla oblongata: cardio-acceleratory, cardio-inhibitory, vasomotor centres
Cardio-inhibitory stimulated; cardio-acceleratory inhibited
Via the vagus nerve: rate and force drop, cardiac output drops
Vasomotor centre: vasodilation, more space for the blood
Blood pressure back down to normal

chapters.title: Case 3, part 3: her four lung micrographs
chapters.scen: Exam case 3 · Asthma — Ane has had severe asthma since they were young. During a particularly bad asthma attack, Ane is experiencing difficulty breathing, particularly on the out-breath. Ane’s asthma is often triggered by small particles of pollen that manage to make their way into their lungs despite the protective features designed to keep them out. Ane makes sure to have their Salbutamol inhaler, which helps to relieve the symptoms of their asthma attack.

show.ask: Her four lung micrographs, A to D (Case Study Workbook, case 3, “Images of different parts of the lungs”): name the part of the airway each one shows, and give its lining and whether cartilage and smooth muscle are present.
show.hook: Cartilage stops at the bronchiole; muscle stops at the alveoli.

t: Trachea: ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Cartilage present; smooth muscles present
Bronchus: ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium (1)
Smooth muscles (2) and cartilage (3) present
Bronchiole: cuboidal epithelium
Cartilage absent; smooth muscles present
Type 1 pneumocytes: squamous epithelium for gaseous exchange
Type 2 for surfactant; macrophages keep them clean
No cartilage or muscles
Bronchodilators relax the muscle (reliever); cortisol daily (preventer)

chapters.title: Case 4, part 1: Manaia's breathing
chapters.scen: Exam case 4 · Panic attacks — Manaia lives with an anxiety disorder, which sometimes manifests in panic attacks that impact on her breathing. Manaia describes her panic attack as a time when she breathes really really hard and fast and cannot control her breathing at all. You know that there is a link between breathing and the pH of your blood because the respiratory system is one of the buffer systems of the body. You know that during a prolonged panic attack, Manaia might be at risk of what is called respiratory alkalosis, but you’ll need to remember why this is.

show.ask: Breathing, or the process of pulmonary ventilation is how you move air in and out of your lungs and requires a specific series of steps. Bullet point the steps involved in Manaia’s inhalation.
show.hook: CONTRACT → BIGGER → LOWER pressure → air IN.

t: The diaphragm contracts (its dome lowers)
The external intercostal muscles contract: ribs up and out
The thoracic cavity enlarges; intrapleural pressure falls (Boyle’s law)
Intrapulmonary volume increases, so its pressure falls
Air flows in, from high pressure to low

show.ask: Bullet point the steps involved in Manaia’s exhalation.
show.hook: RELAX → RECOIL → HIGHER pressure → air OUT.

t: The diaphragm relaxes (its dome rises)
The external intercostals relax: ribs down and in
The elastic lungs recoil passively
Intrapulmonary pressure rises (Boyle’s law)
Air flows out to the lower atmospheric pressure

show.ask: Manaia feels tired after a panic attack because forced breathing requires more muscular effort. Which muscles are used in forced breathing? Be specific!
show.hook: IN: the neck lifts. OUT: the abs and internal intercostals squeeze.

t: At rest: diaphragm and external intercostals contract
Forced: also sternocleidomastoid and scalenes (neck)
Forced: the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals contract

show.ask: What are some of the factors that influence your pulmonary ventilation (make it easier or harder) and how do they do this?
show.hook: BLOCKED airways, STIFF lungs, a LOST pleural seal.

t: Airway obstruction: fluid, mucus, swelling (COPD, asthma)
raises resistance and the muscular effort needed
Less lung compliance: scar tissue, rib cage or diaphragm problems
No surfactant, or fluid in the alveoli
Air in the pleural cavity (pneumothorax) collapses the lung (atelectasis)

chapters.title: Case 4, part 2: breathing and blood pH
chapters.scen: Exam case 4 · Panic attacks — Manaia lives with an anxiety disorder, which sometimes manifests in panic attacks that impact on her breathing. Manaia describes her panic attack as a time when she breathes really really hard and fast and cannot control her breathing at all. You know that there is a link between breathing and the pH of your blood because the respiratory system is one of the buffer systems of the body. You know that during a prolonged panic attack, Manaia might be at risk of what is called respiratory alkalosis, but you’ll need to remember why this is.

show.ask: What is normal blood pH?
show.hook: 7.35 to 7.45: below is acid, above is alkaline.

t: Below 7.35 = acidotic; above 7.45 = alkalotic

show.ask: Draw the chemical equation (in words or chemical formula) for the bicarbonate buffer system in the blood
show.hook: CO₂ + water ⇌ carbonic acid ⇌ H⁺ + bicarbonate.

t: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻
carbon dioxide + water ⇌ carbonic acid ⇌ hydrogen ions + bicarbonate ions

show.ask: How do changes in the respiratory rate and depth (like Manaia’s panic attack) affect the blood pH?
show.hook: Blow off CO₂ → H⁺ FALLS → pH RISES: alkalosis.

t: Rate and depth change the CO₂ in the alveoli and the blood
Blood CO₂ drives the bicarbonate buffer
so H⁺ changes with it, and so does pH
Hyperventilation blows off CO₂ → H⁺ falls → pH rises
This is respiratory alkalosis
(Hypoventilation: CO₂ up, H⁺ up → respiratory acidosis)

show.ask: How does the respiratory system respond when something causes the blood pH to change? (This is back to BN1 when you talked about ketoacidosis!)
show.hook: Too ACID → breathe FASTER. Too ALKALINE → breathe SLOWER.

t: Metabolic acidosis (H⁺ up): hyperventilation
H⁺ becomes CO₂ and water; the extra CO₂ is breathed off
Metabolic alkalosis (H⁺ down): hypoventilation
CO₂ is kept and turned back into H⁺ and bicarbonate

chapters.title: Case 4, part 3: her two acid-base tables
chapters.scen: Exam case 4 · Panic attacks — Manaia lives with an anxiety disorder, which sometimes manifests in panic attacks that impact on her breathing. Manaia describes her panic attack as a time when she breathes really really hard and fast and cannot control her breathing at all. You know that there is a link between breathing and the pH of your blood because the respiratory system is one of the buffer systems of the body. You know that during a prolonged panic attack, Manaia might be at risk of what is called respiratory alkalosis, but you’ll need to remember why this is.

show.ask: Complete the table for metabolic acid/base imbalance: How has blood pH changed? How has H+ levels in the blood changed? How does the bicarbonate buffer system respond? What ultimately happens to CO2 levels in the blood? How does breathing rate change as a result?
show.hook: ACID → the buffer MAKES CO₂ → breathe FASTER. Alkaline → the reverse.

t: Acidosis: H⁺ has increased
Buffer gets rid of H⁺: converting it into CO₂ and water
so CO₂ levels in the blood increase
Breathing rate increases: get rid of that CO₂
Alkalosis: H⁺ has decreased
Buffer replaces the lost H⁺: CO₂ and water → H⁺ and bicarbonate
so CO₂ levels in the blood decrease
Breathing rate decreases: keep that CO₂ in

show.ask: Complete the table for respiratory acid/base imbalance: How has ventilation changed? (Hyper/hypo) How has that changed CO2 levels in the blood? How does the bicarbonate buffer system respond? What ultimately happens to H+ levels in the blood? How does blood pH change as a result?
show.hook: Breathing sets CO₂; H⁺ FOLLOWS CO₂; pH goes the OTHER way.

t: Hyperventilation (Manaia): CO₂ levels decrease
Buffer tries to replace the lost CO₂, using up H⁺ and bicarbonate
so H⁺ levels decrease
Blood pH increases: alkalosis
Hypoventilation (head trauma): CO₂ levels increase
Buffer gets rid of excess CO₂: combining it with water
→ H⁺ and bicarbonate, so H⁺ levels increase
Blood pH decreases: acidosis

show.ask: Compare the tables you completed above – what do you notice?
show.hook: CO₂ and H⁺ move TOGETHER.

t: Very similar processes: the bicarbonate buffer system
CO₂ and H⁺ are linked: whatever happens to one happens to the other

chapters.title: Case 6, part 1: what insulin does
chapters.scen: Exam case 6 · Diabetes — Larry has been recently diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes mellitus, an endocrine disorder, after what appears to be many years of uncontrolled hyperglycaemia. He must measure his blood sugar every as he works with his diabetes nurse to bring it under control, and he will also need to have insulin injections and other medications to help his blood glucose regulation. Larry is a little overwhelmed, and isn’t sure of what this insulin is for. As his nurse, you need a robust understanding of what insulin does in the body. Diabetes mellitus is a disease that involves the dysfunction of insulin and glucose regulation. There are two types, type 1 where the body fails to make insulin, and type 2 where the body is unable to respond to insulin when it is secreted.

show.ask: Where in the body, SPECIFICALLY, is insulin made?
show.hook: Pancreas → islets → BETA cells make insulin (glucAgon = Alpha).

t: The endocrine pancreas
in the islets of Langerhans
Beta cells make insulin, which decreases blood sugar
(Alpha cells make glucagon)

show.ask: What hormone (or hormones!) acts in opposition to insulin, and where is it/they made?
show.hook: GLUCAGON, the stress pair (ADRENALINE, CORTISOL), then GROWTH and THYROID.

groups.h: The hormones and where they are made
t: Glucagon: the pancreas alpha cells
Adrenaline (adrenal medulla) and cortisol (adrenal cortex)
both mediate the stress response, which needs ready glucose
Growth hormone (anterior pituitary) and thyroid hormones

show.ask: Explain what insulin does at a cellular level (you’ll need to think about how it travels in the body, what it binds to, and what happens).
show.hook: TRAVEL, BIND, MOVE GLUT4, LET GLUCOSE IN.

t: Insulin travels in the blood
It binds to insulin receptors on the cell surface
A cascade moves GLUT4 into the cell membrane
GLUT4 lets glucose in, down its concentration gradient
by facilitated diffusion

show.ask: Insulin’s role in the liver is:
show.hook: Liver and muscle STORE glucose as GLYCOGEN.

t: Glucose → glycogen, by glycogenesis

show.ask: Insulin’s role in the muscles is:
show.hook: Same as the liver: glucose into GLYCOGEN.

t: Glucose → glycogen, by glycogenesis

show.ask: Insulin’s role in the fat tissue is:
show.hook: Fat tissue turns glucose into FAT: LIPOgenesis.

t: Glucose → fats, by lipogenesis
the most efficient storage form

show.ask: *Insulin's role in the liver is to stimulate it to stimulate ____. *Insulin's role in the muscle cells is to stimulate them to ____. *Insulin's role in the fat tissue is to stimulate ____. Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis are stimulated by the hormone (s) ____. Glycogenesis is stimulated by the hormone ____. Glycogenolysis is stimulated by the hormone ____.

t: 1. convert glucose to glycogen
2. insert GLUT 4 receptors into the membrane to facilitate glucose uptake
3. lipogenesis
4. glucagon and epinephrine
5. insulin
6. glucagon

chapters.title: Case 6, part 2: glucagon, the day graph, and the tired pancreas
chapters.scen: Exam case 6 · Diabetes — Larry has been recently diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes mellitus, an endocrine disorder, after what appears to be many years of uncontrolled hyperglycaemia. He must measure his blood sugar every as he works with his diabetes nurse to bring it under control, and he will also need to have insulin injections and other medications to help his blood glucose regulation. Larry is a little overwhelmed, and isn’t sure of what this insulin is for. As his nurse, you need a robust understanding of what insulin does in the body. Diabetes mellitus is a disease that involves the dysfunction of insulin and glucose regulation. There are two types, type 1 where the body fails to make insulin, and type 2 where the body is unable to respond to insulin when it is secreted.

show.ask: What other molecules also influence blood glucose levels?
show.hook: Glucagon RAISES BGL three ways: glycogen, fat, new glucose.

t: Glucagon: breaks down glycogen (glycogenolysis)
Breaks down fats (lipolysis)
Liver: gluconeogenesis, new glucose from non-glucose sources

show.ask: Insulin is designed to only be high after a meal, so in normal function it shows a pattern like the accompanying diagram. Can you describe the normal BGL over the day? What about insulin?
show.hook: Spikes after MEALS; never zero; basal underneath, bolus on top.

t: BGL follows your meals (carbs and sugar)
Background insulin: insulin is never at zero
BGL never zero either: stays in the normal range
Basal = background; bolus = after meals

show.ask: In normal blood sugar regulation, does BGL go above the normal range?
show.hook: No.

t: No: it should not exceed the normal range

show.ask: What happens overnight? What could that mean for the morning?
show.hook: Lowest at night; break the FAST in the morning.

t: BGL is lowest overnight
Breakfast = breaking the fast: hungry, glycogen run out

show.ask: When the body cells are resistant to the insulin signal, the pancreas tries to compensate by making MORE insulin, to make the signal meaningful again. Due to all this pancreas hyperactivity, damage and loss of function can occur, which means the pancreas now struggles to make enough insulin. What would happen in the body now? How might we need to intervene?
show.hook: Overworked pancreas → too little insulin → type 2 on insulin.

t: Pancreatic fatigue: damage from overworking
Low insulin: impaired glucose regulation
Type 2 diabetes: may end up on insulin

chapters.title: Case 8, part 1: the joint, A to H
chapters.scen: Exam case 8 · Joints and arthritis — Shannon is a 30-year-old woman that has had a series of issues with her joints. She has had bursitis in her hip in the past, and is now has presented mainly with pain in her knee and hip joints, as well as her hands. After consultation, she has recently been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. She is concerned, as she feels she is too young to have arthritis, even though she is fairly active and has been an athlete most of her life. Part of the treatment plan that manage the joint includes the use of prednisone. Prednisone is a synthetic corticosteroid, similar to cortisol. Cortisol is part of the body’s long term stress response.

show.ask: Arthritis is a condition that affects the joints of the body. What are the structures of the joint? Use the diagram and name the lettered structures, with the function of each.
show.hook: Muscle, enthesis, fluid, bursa, capsule, tendon, bone, cartilage, ligament.

t: A: muscle, contracts to move the bones
A (the other two): enthesis, where the ligaments attach
B: synovial fluid, lubricates the joint
C: bursa, reduces friction
D: joint capsule, holds the bones together
E: tendon, joins muscle to bone
F: bone, a lever that articulates at joints
G: hyaline cartilage, reduces friction and absorbs shock
H: ligament, holds bones together

show.ask: The knee and hip are both synovial joints. What are the benefits to the body of a synovial joint?
show.hook: FREELY movable: without them, very little movement.

t: Synovial joints are freely movable
The most freely moving joints: without them, very limited movement

show.ask: What kind of synovial joint are the hip and knee? The shoulder and the elbow?
show.hook: Ball-and-socket: shoulder, HIP. Hinge, like a door: KNEE, elbow.

t: Shoulder and hip: ball-and-socket
Knee and elbow: hinge, open and close like a door

show.ask: What is bursitis?
show.hook: A friction CUSHION that gets inflamed.

t: Bursa: a fluid-filled sac between bone and soft tissue
A cushion to reduce friction
Inflamed and swollen: the opposite effect, and painful

show.ask: 1. The part labeled B in the diagram is known as ____ and is responsible for ____ the joint. 2. The part labeled G in the diagram is known as ____ and is NOT responsible for ____ the joint. 3. The labeled part that is affected primarily by arthritis is labelled ____. Osteoarthritis occurs most often in ____.

t: 1. synovial fluid
2. lubricating
3. hyaline cartilage
4. secreting synovial fluid
6. elderly because of wear and tear

show.ask: Compare and contrast bursitis and arthritis. (her answer is not posted yet)

t: Both: inflammation, with pain and swelling around a joint
Bursitis: the bursa, a fluid-filled sac outside the joint; often from overuse or pressure; usually settles
Arthritis: the joint itself, wearing the articular cartilage and inflaming the synovial membrane; usually long-term

chapters.title: Case 8, part 2: rheumatoid arthritis, cortisol, and Shannon
chapters.scen: Exam case 8 · Joints and arthritis — Shannon is a 30-year-old woman that has had a series of issues with her joints. She has had bursitis in her hip in the past, and is now has presented mainly with pain in her knee and hip joints, as well as her hands. After consultation, she has recently been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. She is concerned, as she feels she is too young to have arthritis, even though she is fairly active and has been an athlete most of her life. Part of the treatment plan that manage the joint includes the use of prednisone. Prednisone is a synthetic corticosteroid, similar to cortisol. Cortisol is part of the body’s long term stress response.

show.ask: What occurs in rheumatoid arthritis?
show.hook: AUTOIMMUNE, FAST, BOTH SIDES, WHOLE BODY.

t: Autoimmune: the immune system attacks the joints
Onset is relatively rapid, over weeks to months, at any age
Joints painful, swollen and stiff, on both sides of the body
Morning stiffness longer than 1 hour
Whole-body symptoms: fatigue, feeling ill

show.ask: What is the other type of arthritis called?
show.hook: OSTEO-arthritis: the wear-and-tear one.

t: Osteoarthritis

show.ask: What is the difference between the above and rheumatoid arthritis?
show.hook: Cause, onset, joints, whole body: rheumatoid is immune, fast, both sides, systemic.

t: Rheumatoid: autoimmune; osteo: wear and tear
Rheumatoid: any age, weeks to months; osteo: later in life, over years
Rheumatoid: swollen, symmetrical, stiffness over 1 hour
Osteo: ache, little swelling, one set of joints, under 1 hour
Rheumatoid has whole body symptoms; osteo does not

show.ask: Where is cortisol produced and secreted from the body?
show.hook: Adrenal CORTEX, on the kidney, told by ACTH.

t: The adrenal glands, on top of the kidneys
in the adrenal cortex (the outer part)
ACTH from the anterior pituitary

show.ask: What are the functions of cortisol and how is this related to the stress response?
show.hook: More SUGAR, steady BLOOD VOLUME, LESS inflammation.

t: Increases blood glucose by gluconeogenesis
and raises blood fatty acids and amino acids
Reduces inflammation and suppresses the immune system
Helps resist chronic (long-term) stress: steady blood sugar
Keeps up blood volume, so tissue perfusion continues

show.ask: How is cortisol going to aid in Shannon’s rheumatoid arthritis?
show.hook: Calms the SWELLING, calms the IMMUNE attack.

t: Reduces inflammation: less swelling, redness and pain
Suppresses the immune system: RA is autoimmune

show.ask: What might you say to Shannon about her concerns?
show.hook: RA is autoimmune: ANY age.

t: Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune: it can hit at any age
Not the wear and tear of osteoarthritis, which begins later in life

chapters.title: Case 9, part 1: neurotransmitters and the synapse
chapters.scen: Exam case 9 · Neurotransmitters and the brain — Mr Paraone has been admitted to hospital after a fall and has reported they are having issues with mobility and tremors. Mr Paraone is later diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. This is a brain disease where cells that normally make Dopamine, a neurotransmitter, start to die. One of the treatments to help control their symptoms is called Levodopa, which travels through the blood and into the brain to help to boost the brain’s Dopamine levels, so the neurons can continue to communicate properly via their synapses.

show.ask: What is a neurotransmitter? Where is the neurotransmitter Dopamine normally made in the central nervous system?
show.hook: A chemical across the synapse; dopamine from the SUBSTANTIA NIGRA.

t: A chemical released at the presynaptic endings of a chemical synapse
It acts on the receptor region of the postsynaptic neuron
Dopamine: the substantia nigra of the midbrain

show.ask: Explain the role of Calcium ions (Ca2+) in synaptic transmission.
show.hook: Impulse ARRIVES → Ca²⁺ IN → vesicles RELEASE.

t: The action potential reaches the axon terminal
Ca2+ channels open; Ca2+ enters the presynaptic neuron
Ca2+ opens the vesicles: neurotransmitter out by exocytosis

show.ask: Explain the process of synaptic transmission that allows neurotransmitters to be released. Use the diagram to help you in your explanation.
show.hook: ARRIVE, CALCIUM, RELEASE, CROSS, BIND, RESPOND, CLEAR.

t: The action potential reaches the axon terminal
Ca2+ enters the presynaptic neuron
Vesicles release it into the synaptic cleft (exocytosis)
It diffuses across the synaptic cleft
It binds to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron
Permeability changes: excitatory or inhibitory
Then re-uptake or enzymatic destruction

show.ask: When neurotransmitters bind to a receptor, what happens?
show.hook: The gate changes: EXCITE or INHIBIT.

t: The postsynaptic membrane’s permeability changes
Excitatory or inhibitory: stimulated or inhibited

show.ask: After the neurotransmitter has been released, what happens to that chemical signal?
show.hook: Take it BACK or BREAK it down.

t: Re-uptake into the presynaptic neuron
or enzymatic destruction

chapters.title: Case 9, part 2: label the synapse, and why levodopa
chapters.scen: Exam case 9 · Neurotransmitters and the brain — Mr Paraone has been admitted to hospital after a fall and has reported they are having issues with mobility and tremors. show.ask: Label her synapse figure, A to G, and name the two transport processes it shows.
show.hook: VESICLES mean pre (F); RECEPTORS mean post (G).

t: A: calcium channel
B: vesicle
C: neurotransmitter molecules
D: reuptake channel
E: receptors
F: presynaptic neuron (the vesicles)
G: postsynaptic neuron (the receptors)
Exocytosis: the vesicle fuses, releasing the neurotransmitter
Diffusion across the synaptic cleft

show.ask: 1. B is pointing towards a vesicle containing ____. 2. E shows ____. 3. The transport process moving neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft is ____ and over the synaptic cleft is ____.

t: 1. Neurotransmitters such as serotonin, epinephrine or dopamine
2. A receptor on the post synaptic membrane
3. exocytosis
4. Simple diffusion

show.ask: Levodopa, which travels through the blood and into the brain is used as medication. Why not Dopamine itself?
show.hook: Only what crosses the BLOOD-BRAIN BARRIER works on the brain.

t: Must cross the blood-brain barrier to work on brain cells
Not fat soluble: cannot cross, useless for the brain
Levodopa crosses, becomes dopamine; dopamine itself does not cross

chapters.title: Case 10: stroke, and the map of the brain
chapters.scen: Exam case 10 · Stroke and the brain — You are working in a stroke rehabilitation unit, and are often interacting with individuals that are recovering from stroke, cerebrovascular accident, when parts of the brain are damaged during periods of ischaemia. Different areas of the brain control different tasks, so the symptoms a person shows, or the functions they have lost will be reflective of the part of their brain that has been damaged by the ischaemia. You are working with a range of people with differing functions, and you’re thinking about what parts of the brains must be involved.

show.ask: Review the functional regions of the cerebrum using this image: name the functional area at each letter, A to G.
show.hook: A to G: PLAN, SPEAK, MOVE, FEEL, HEAR, UNDERSTAND, SEE.

t: A: prefrontal cortex
B: Broca’s area
C: motor area, precentral gyrus
D: somatosensory area, postcentral gyrus
E: auditory area
F: Wernicke’s area
G: occipital (visual) area

show.ask: For each region, brainstorm the possible changes to function or behaviour that would result from damage to that region.
show.hook: Lose what it does: judgement, speech, movement, touch, hearing, understanding, sight.

t: A prefrontal: poor judgement, inappropriate behaviour, loss of focus
B Broca’s: difficulty producing speech and writing
C motor: loss of voluntary movement
D somatosensory: loss of touch and general sensation
E auditory: hearing affected
F Wernicke’s: cannot understand language
G occipital: vision affected

chapters.title: Case 13, part 1: the kit, ovulation, and the cycle graph
chapters.scen: Exam case 13 · Fertility — Rose and Simon are seeing the nurse at their local GP’s clinic, as they have recently made the decision to begin trying to conceive. Rose has been on the Depo Provera injection as a method of contraception for the past 2 years. As her nurse, you advise that it could take a little while for her normal cycle to settle after coming off this hormonal contraceptive. Rose takes your recommendation about tracking her cycle after learning that there are limited days in the month where she will be fertile and able to conceive. She has also taken your recommendation about purchasing an ovulation predictor kit and some pregnancy tests.

show.ask: What is an ovulation predictor kit? What does it show?
show.hook: It catches the LH PEAK in urine.

t: When ovulation is about to happen
It picks up the peak in luteinizing hormone (LH) in the urine

show.ask: What occurs during ovulation?
show.hook: LH PEAK → follicle BURSTS → oocyte OUT → toward the FIMBRIAE.

t: A secondary oocyte is released from the ovary
Triggered by a peak in LH
The Graafian (tertiary) follicle bursts; the ovarian wall ruptures
Fluid pushes the oocyte to the fimbriae of the Fallopian tube

show.ask: What days of a female’s cycle are they fertile? Use the accompanying image to answer.
show.hook: Days 10 to 17.

t: Days 10–17

show.ask: Can you explain why the hormone levels change over the course of the menstrual cycle?
show.hook: Each hormone has a job: FSH grows, estrogen thickens, LH releases, progesterone prepares.

t: Each hormone drives a different process
Follicles develop (FSH); the uterine lining thickens (estrogen)
Ovulation (LH); ready for implantation (progesterone)

show.ask: How would pregnancy change the hormone levels graph?
show.hook: No DROP at day 21: the levels keep RISING.

t: The hormone drop at about day 21 does not happen
Estrogen and progesterone keep rising

chapters.title: Case 13, part 2: contraception, and the three she hasn't answered
chapters.scen: Exam case 13 · Fertility — Rose and Simon are seeing the nurse at their local GP’s clinic, as they have recently made the decision to begin trying to conceive. Rose has been on the Depo Provera injection as a method of contraception for the past 2 years. Rose takes your recommendation about tracking her cycle after learning that there are limited days in the month where she will be fertile and able to conceive. She has also taken your recommendation about purchasing an ovulation predictor kit and some pregnancy tests.

show.ask: Hormonal methods of contraception tend to impact a female’s fertility by using progesterone. Describe how we use the normal functions of the hormone progesterone to prevent pregnancy?
show.hook: STOP ovulation, BLOCK the sperm, FAKE a pregnancy.

t: Prevents ovulation: stops the LH being released
Thickens the cervical mucus: keeps the sperm out
Imitates pregnancy: keeps progesterone levels high

show.ask: Contraception can be hormonal or non-hormonal. Summarise the differences in a tabular form. (Method · How does this prevent pregnancy? · Does this prevent STI?)
show.hook: Hormones STOP OVULATION; a condom is a BARRIER; only the CONDOM stops STIs.

t: The pill, the Jadelle implant: may prevent ovulation
Mini pill: stops LH, thickens cervical mucus, imitates pregnancy
STIs? No: pregnancy only, there is no barrier
Condoms: a barrier keeps the semen out
Protect against pregnancy and STIs, but not pubic lice
IUD: may prevent implantation in the endometrium
Pregnancy only: only the condom also stops STIs

show.ask: Male and female fertility are different: what are some of the key factors in male and female fertility? (her answer is not posted yet)

t: Male: enough sperm that move well and are the right shape; FSH, LH and testosterone; testes kept cooler than the body
Female: age; regular ovulation (FSH, LH, oestrogen, progesterone in balance); open fallopian tubes; a healthy uterine lining
Both: smoking, alcohol, weight, stress and STIs lower fertility; after Depo Provera the cycle can take months to return

show.ask: What are the functions of the sex hormones in the human body? (her answer is not posted yet)

t: FSH: grows the follicles; drives spermatogenesis
LH: triggers ovulation and forms the corpus luteum; makes the Leydig cells produce testosterone
Oestrogen: follicle growth, reproductive organs, breasts, hips, pelvis; rebuilds the endometrium (proliferative phase)
Progesterone: readies the endometrium for implantation (secretory phase); develops the breast alveoli in pregnancy
Testosterone: spermatogenesis, male secondary sex characteristics, muscle, bone, libido

show.ask: Injections of FSH usually form part of IVF. What is IVF, when would it be appropriate, and what is the purpose of the FSH injections? (her answer is not posted yet)

t: IVF, in vitro fertilisation: eggs are collected and fertilised by sperm in a lab, and the embryo is placed in the uterus
When: blocked or damaged fallopian tubes, low sperm count or movement, ovulation problems, endometriosis, unexplained infertility
FSH injections: make several follicles grow at once, so several eggs can be collected

chapters.title: Case 14, part 1: rods, cones, and red-green colour blindness
chapters.scen: Exam case 14 · RG colour blindness — Simon is colour blind, a condition which affects his ability to distinguish between colours, with the most impact on red and green. He has expressed an interest in understanding why he has the disease, but neither of his parents do. He’s also heard that it is more common in males and so is wondering if he will pass this disease onto any sons he might have.

show.ask: What is red-green colour blindness? (Distinguish between cones and rods, specifically where they are found in the eye; distinguish their functions using photopic, scotopic, colour, central and peripheral vision; define RG colour blindness in terms of the “inability to observe certain light frequencies”.)
show.hook: Cones see COLOUR; RG = faulty L (red) and M (green) cones.

t: Cones: colour, central vision, in good light, more detailed
Rods: grey scale, more sensitive to light, work in dim light
Macula: cones and rods; fovea: only cones
A genetic defect (an anomaly) of the cones of the retina
Faulty L cones (red, long wavelength) and M cones (green, medium)
Detected with a colour-blindness test
Cones = photopic, colour, central; rods = scotopic, peripheral

chapters.title: Case 14, part 2: Simon's family
chapters.scen: Exam case 14 · RG colour blindness — Simon is colour blind, a condition which affects his ability to distinguish between colours, with the most impact on red and green. He has expressed an interest in understanding why he has the disease, but neither of his parents do. He’s also heard that it is more common in males and so is wondering if he will pass this disease onto any sons he might have.

show.ask: Draw a pedigree chart to show Simon, his mum, his dad, his maternal grandmother (not colour-blind), maternal grandfather (colour-blind), maternal aunt (colour-blind) and maternal uncle (not colour-blind). Can you track how Simon inherited the disease when neither of his parents are colour blind?
show.hook: Grandad’s Xb → carrier MUM → Simon XbY; his dad gives only a Y.

t: Grandfather: XbY (a colour-blind man)
Grandmother: XBXb, a carrier (she has a colour-blind daughter)
Aunt: XbXb (the defect on both X chromosomes)
Uncle: XBY (not colour-blind)
Mum: XBXb, a carrier; her XB gives normal vision
Dad: XBY, he has the normal X
Simon: XbY; Xb from his mum, only a Y from dad

show.ask: Given the above and your own research, how is red-green colour blindness inherited?
show.hook: X-linked RECESSIVE: carrier mums, affected sons; dads never to sons.

t: X-linked recessive: the L and M cone genes are on the X
Carried by mothers, shows in 50% of their sons
Shows only when all X chromosomes are affected: a woman needs both
Can skip a generation
Never to their sons: sons get only a Y
Always the affected X to all their daughters

show.ask: Will Simon pass on red-green colour blindness to his children? How?
show.hook: Sons get his Y (clear); daughters get his Xb (carriers).

t: None of his sons: they get his Y
All his daughters, as unaffected carriers: they get his X

show.ask: What would Simon's mum's genotype have been and why do you say so?

t: XbXB - she carried it over to Simon but her normal XB gave her normal vision

show.ask: Will Simon pass on red-green colour-blindness to his children? How?

t: To none of his sons, but to all his daughters who will be unaffected carriers

chapters.title: Case 15: cystic fibrosis, Huntington's, and the two whānau
chapters.scen: Exam case 15 · Genetic diseases — You’ve been working in a GP clinic, working alongside many different families, serving a rural community. Recently, you’ve been working alongside two families that have genetic diseases. One family has cystic fibrosis (the Harris whanau), and one has Huntington’s disease (the Anderson whanau). You are wanting to understand more about how these diseases are passed from person to person, and how this might affect any future children that are born into these families.

show.ask: What are the modes of inheritance of Huntington’s disease and Cystic Fibrosis? Explain the modes of inheritance for both diseases (chromosome type, pattern of inheritance, what this means).
show.hook: CF: autosomal RECESSIVE, rr, skips generations. HD: autosomal DOMINANT, every generation.

t: Autosomal recessive, on chromosome 7
Skips generations; people can be carriers
Affected person: rr
Autosomal dominant, on chromosome 4
Shows whenever the dominant allele is present: every generation
Affected person: Rr or RR

show.ask: For the pedigree chart of the Harris whānau, state the genotype and phenotype of every person. (her answer is not posted yet)

t: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive: every affected person is rr
Unaffected parents of an affected child are carriers: Rr
Unaffected children of two carriers: RR or Rr
Phenotype: affected, or unaffected (carrier)

show.ask: There are two sisters who are the youngest members of this whānau. What is the chance they could pass this condition on to their children? What circumstances would have to occur? (her answer is not posted yet)

t: A child is affected only if BOTH parents pass on an r
So the sister must carry r, and so must her partner
Carrier × carrier (Rr × Rr): 25% affected, 50% carriers
Affected sister (rr) × carrier: 50% for each child; × RR partner: 0% affected

show.ask: For the pedigree chart of the Anderson whānau, state the genotype and phenotype of every person. (her answer is not posted yet)

t: Huntington's is autosomal dominant: every affected person is Hh (rarely HH)
Every unaffected person is hh
No healthy carriers; every affected person has an affected parent

show.ask: There are 6 cousins in the youngest generation of this whānau. What is the chance that they could pass this condition on to their children? (her answer is not posted yet)

t: An unaffected cousin (hh): 0%, no H to pass on
An affected cousin (Hh) with an hh partner: 50% for each child
